 A year after SNAP cuts, Nebraska families and food banks are feeling the strain
 By Macy Byars , Reporter Nebraska Public Media News
 Oct. 20, 2026, 1:16 p.m. · 
 At Matt Talbot, visits to the center’s Fresh Choice Pantry jumped 96% between January and July. (Hannah Nazarenus/Nebraska Public Media News) 
 Listen To This Story
 One year ago, Nebraska implemented federal eligibility changes for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. Since then, Nebraskans facing food insecurity are having a harder time making ends meet, and advocates are calling for a rollback of the changes.
 The number of households participating in SNAP dropped about 23% in Nebraska between October 2025 and August 2026. That’s according to data published monthly by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, which administers the SNAP program.
 Nebraska Appleseed hosted a virtual roundtable Tuesday – the one-year anniversary of the changes – to share the impact on food bank leaders, community groups and people living without SNAP benefits.
 “The number of Nebraskans who have lost SNAP since HR1 passed is bigger than the entire population of Kearney,” said Eric Savaiano, who runs Nebraska Appleseed’s food and nutrition access program. “The number of children who have lost SNAP in just one year exceeds the populations of Scottsbluff or La Vista.”
 That’s about 17,000 households or 37,000 individuals no longer participating in SNAP.
 Savaiano said most of those losses are due to more stringent work requirements and the paperwork associated with them.
 “Since these new verification requirements have gone into effect, thousands of eligible people have been cut off benefits,” he said. “Call center wait times have skyrocketed, and application processing timelines have increased dramatically.”
 Community impact 
 Eligibility changes to the SNAP program were passed in July 2025 through the Republican-led tax and spending bill, or HR1.
 Work requirements were expanded under the bill. Able-bodied adults 55-64 and those with dependents 14 and older were no longer exempt. Exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youths were also struck.
 Joan Jakoubek is a Navy veteran and mother of two. When the requirements started, she was only working 15 hours a week.
 “I struggle with arthritis in my right hip and limited mobility from a workplace injury. I would have needed to quit that job and attempt to find and secure a new job that would allow me to have enough hours,” she said. “Finding that new employment that could accommodate my mobility needs – I just didn’t have time to do it.”
 Jakoubek and her children were also facing homelessness.
 “As someone who lived in a hotel with my children for five months last year without any other options, I can say firsthand how important SNAP is to people who are struggling with housing stability,” she said “When you're in constant survival mode, trying to struggle with how the roof is going to be covered and the food is going to be covered … Food security took on another form for us while we were homeless.”
 Now in VA housing, Jakoubek said she believes other families have it worse.
 “But that's precisely why I think it's important for us to bring this to light, so that our leaders know – what does it say about us as Nebraskans if we can't give back to the people like me and others who've served our country?” she said.
 Most non-citizens were no longer eligible as soon as the bill was passed, though states implemented the changes on varying timelines.
 Hannah Vlach Perez is the executive director of Restoring Dignity, an Omaha nonprofit serving refugee families. She said about 2,350 refugees in the city have lost SNAP benefits since Nebraska’s October 2025 implementation.
 “SNAP was not a reward for being a refugee,” Vlach Perez said. “Families had to qualify based on their financial circumstances, and the families that are on SNAP are the families that are struggling the most.”
 Restoring Dignity started the Feed a Family program, where donors would contribute monthly to help refugee families afford food. Now, said Vlach Perez, rising costs for all families are putting the program in jeopardy.
 “I keep getting email notifications of people every week, saying ‘I'm sorry, I'm going to have to cancel my plan. I can't afford it anymore,’” she said. “I feel like that's an indicator of where things are going, and we're worried that people aren't going to be able to give money, as much money, anymore because they're having to pay so much more for gas and food and everything.”
 Food banks began seeing an uptick in need immediately.
 “Last fiscal year, our food banks combined served 2.7 million duplicate individuals in Nebraska through our programs and partnerships,” said President and CEO of the Food Bank of Lincoln Michaella Kumke. “That was a 45% increase from five years ago.”
 The need has stayed high.
 Right now, Kumke said, most food banks are able to meet the needs of their communities. However, continued high demand could make it harder to meet those needs in the future.
 “We are craving true partnership with state agencies and federal policy to deliver quality support for our neighbors,” she said. “Our neighbors are going hungry, and until a partnership is realized, more neighbors will go hungry.”
 Stephanie Sullivan, assistant director of marketing and communications at Food Bank for the Heartland said charitable giving can’t fully replace SNAP.
 “SNAP can only work when it works in tandem with food banks and food pantries,” she told Nebraska Public Media News. “But when you remove that support system, you cannot expect food banks to cover that need. And, in fact, we are not meeting the need.”
 Sullivan said many people visiting food banks have never visited before, and demand is higher than it was during the COVID-19 pandemic. Costs are also rising for the Food Bank of the Heartland to distribute food to pantries across Nebraska, and federal support is declining .
 “We're expecting just the rise in fuel to add an additional $10,000 to our operating budget this year,” Sullivan said. “It's costing us more to deliver the food, and it's also costing us more to get food, and that is a formula that's never going to add up. It means less food for more people.”
 Though Sullivan said the generosity of Nebraskans has helped keep pantries stocked, she worries the continued demand could further stress the system.
 “For every meal a food bank can provide, SNAP provides nine ,” she said. “So, it is unimaginable to think that a food bank could make up for the loss of SNAP, because we simply cannot.”
 More cuts on the way for states 
 States may need to absorb some of the cost to run SNAP due to new requirements around cost sharing. If a state’s error rate – a number calculated from both underpayments and overpayments – is too high, the federal government will provide less money for SNAP benefits.
 Nebraska’s error rate is below HR1’s 6% threshold and will not have to pay into providing benefits. It was 5.9% in fiscal year 2025. In 2029, if Nebraska’s rate is over 6%, it will be subject to cost share requirements.
 Savaiano worries that topping that 6% error rate would ultimately lead to the closure of the state’s SNAP program.
 “It'll mean the state has fewer dollars to put toward administrative expenses like keeping our error rate low, and then we will have even more penalties to pay, ultimately ending in our state ending the SNAP program overall,” Savaiano said.
 In a statement to Nebraska Public Media News, Nebraska DHHS said the wait times were "temporary" as it works to keep the state's error rate low with additional "documentation verification."
 "DHHS is aggressively recruiting and hiring staff, which will soon alleviate workloads and improve processing times, which will also reduce call volume and wait times," an agency spokesperson wrote. "Providing timely, effective customer service remains a top priority for DHHS, and we continually monitor call center performance and customer feedback to identify opportunities for improvement and better serve Nebraskans."
 The agency said it would cost Nebraska between $20 million and $25 million if the error rate crossed 6%.
 Nebraska DHHS said it continues to work with applicants throughout the new process. It also connects applicants with skill and job training through its SNAP Employment & Training program, which includes help with job searching and interview preparation.
 All states are now required to pay for 75% of SNAP’s administrative costs under HR1. Costs were previously split 50-50 between state and federal dollars.
 In the most recent budget request by Nebraska DHHS, the agency asked for $9.5 million more in state funds to cover extra administrative costs for 2028 and 2029.
 Nebraska Appleseed and other advocacy groups are calling for a rollback of SNAP cuts and eligibility changes.
 “We cannot balance our budget on the backs of hungry Nebraskans, and especially not hungry children. We must protect our most vulnerable and live up to our Nebraska values,” Savaiano said.
 Savaiano said the Nebraska Legislature could “limit the damage” by loosening paperwork requirements and regulating DHHS’ application process. He also suggests state funds could be used to fund food benefits for non-citizens and support food banks.
 As Nebraska faces a budget shortfall, all state agencies are being asked to cut their budgets by 8% over the next two fiscal years.
